name: Import page
description: The screen that takes a spreadsheet into the system: the file and the rules stated before it is picked, the column mapping, the review of what the system understood, the failures grouped by kind, and the write itself with a report at the end.
when_to_use: A file of records the user hands over once — an item master, a vendor list, opening stock, a rate contract price list, a month of ledger entries. The overlap that matters is form-page's wizard variant, and it is real: both are staged screens with a review at the end. The line is what is being staged. form-page/wizard steps through fields the user types, so the review is a summary of their own answers and the failure mode is field validation. An import steps through stages of a machine's understanding of a file somebody else wrote, so the user is supervising a translation rather than entering data — which is why the middle stage is a mapping grid that has no analogue in a form, why the review is a table of the system's guesses rather than a recap of the user's, and why the failure mode is a data-quality report about 37 rows out of 1,240 rather than a list of controls that are wrong. If you can name every field on screen at design time, it is form-page. Against attachment: that is a document stapled to a record — a signed challan, a test certificate — which is kept, versioned and downloaded for the rest of the record's life. The file on this page is consumed and thrown away; what survives is the rows it created, and the staged copy is deleted a week later. If the user will ever want the file back, it is an attachment and not an import. Where the user goes to see what the import produced is index-page, and the last thing this screen does is send them there. A screen that shows one array of records with a search box and a pager is data-table; a table of rows with a sortable header and nothing around it is table.
rules: This renders inside app-shell, like every signed-in page. The variants start at the Alpine wrapper and their first structural element is <main>; the shell owns the skip link, the nav landmark and the keyboard shortcuts.

The errors are the screen. A clean import is four clicks nobody remembers; what people live through is row 418's UOM reading Kgs when the master says KG, a duplicate item code, a date Excel turned into 45,904, and a vendor that does not exist yet. Every decision in this entry — grouping failures by kind rather than listing them by row, stating the rule once per group instead of once per row, offering the rejected rows as a file — comes from that stage being the one the screen is actually for.

An import is a write, and a half-finished write is the worst outcome, so the page says which of the two contracts it is honouring and says it in the same words on every stage. All-or-nothing: nothing appears in the master until every row has posted, and cancelling discards what has been written. Partial: the good rows post and the rest come back as a file. A user who cannot tell which they got runs the import again, and the second run is the defect.

Partial is never the default and never silent. It is a radio the user chooses at the review stage, against a stated count — post the 1,203 and skip the 37 — because a master that quietly imported 97% of a price list is harder to notice than one that refused, and the 3% it dropped keep last month's rate until somebody spots it.

Rows are matched on a key and the key is named on screen. Item code here; a GRN number, a vendor code, a ledger voucher elsewhere. It is what decides whether a row is a create or an update, and it is what makes a second run of the same file safe to describe: it will update the rows it made rather than duplicating them. Without a named key, "will this run twice" has no answer and the result screen cannot make a promise.

The mapping grid is the stage with no analogue in a form. One row per column in the file, their header and a sample value on one side, a select of your fields on the other, the system's guess already chosen, and a real answer for a column you do not want — Do not import — rather than leaving it blank and hoping. A blank select and a deliberate exclusion look identical and mean opposite things.

Say how each guess was made. Matched on the header name and Guessed from Rate/Kg are different levels of confidence, and a grid that shows eight confident-looking selects invites the user to press Continue without reading any of them. The guessed ones are the only rows anybody needs to check.

The preview shows values as they will be stored, with the file's own text under anything that changed. KG under Kgs, 04 Sep 2026 under 45904, 39012000 under 3901 2000. A preview that echoes the file back confirms the upload and nothing else; the whole question at that stage is whether the translation is right.

Fixing in place is offered only where the fix is a value translation the system can apply to the whole file and remember for the next one — Kgs means KG for this vendor, now and in September. Per-cell editing is offered for the handful of cells where the file is right and the formatting is not. Everything structural goes back to the spreadsheet: 37 hand-edits are 37 ways for the staged copy to differ from the file the vendor sent, and next month the same file arrives with the same 37 rows. The other answer is defensible and this entry does not pretend otherwise — for one typo in 1,240 rows, sending the user back costs them the whole mapping again, which is why a second upload resumes at the review stage with the mapping already applied.

A commit in flight has a known denominator, so it is progress and not spinner: 742 of 1,203 rows. The bar takes no aria-live — a value repainting every few hundred milliseconds queues announcements faster than they can be spoken — and milestones go into a separate role="status" that was in the document before the run started.

What the user may and may not do during the write is written on the screen, not implied by which buttons are grey. They may leave the page. They may not upload the file again. Cancel means something specific under each contract and the sentence changes with it.

The result screen is the one that has to be unambiguous, so it carries four figures and not one: created, updated, not posted, and the total it was given. 1,203 posted is ambiguous on its own — it does not say whether the other 37 were skipped, rejected or never read.

The rejected rows come back as a file with the same columns the user sent plus a Problem column, because the correction happens in the spreadsheet and a list on a web page cannot be pasted back into one.

One h1 and it does not change between stages. The stage nav says where you are; a page whose title changes from Import items to Import complete is a different document arriving under the same URL, and the heading outline stops being usable as a landmark.

The snippet root is a bounded scroller — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box, and the cancel dialog is absolute inset-0 against that frame. As a real page it is the shell's <main>: drop the wrapper's height and border, keep the max-width and the padding, let the footer bar stick to the viewport, and make the dialog fixed inset-0.

anatomy.description: page-header's block: the trail, the one h1, and a line naming the file and its row count once it exists. Never sticky, and never restated per stage.

An <ol> of four stages carrying aria-current="step", the same shape form-page/wizard uses. Stages passed are buttons back, stages ahead are disabled, and below sm the whole thing is one line of text over a thin rail.
One sentence, in the footer bar of every stage, saying whether the rows post together or separately. The same words each time — a paraphrase reads as a different promise.
attachment's zone unchanged: a real file input hidden with sr-only, its label as the peer carrying the focus outline, both drag handlers prevented and the depth counted rather than flagged.
What the file has to be, before the picker rather than after it — the types, the size, the header row, the required columns and a template to download.
One row per column in the file: their header with a sample value, a select of your fields with the guess chosen, and how the guess was made. Below md it is one card per column.
table's markup with the stored value on the first line of each cell and the file's own text under it wherever the two differ, plus an Action column saying create or update.
A <section> per kind of failure: an h3 with the count, the rule stated once, a small table of row numbers and offending cells, and the fix. Not one row per line of the file.
The radio pair that picks the contract when there are failures — post nothing, or post the good rows and report the rest — each with its consequence written under it.
progress's bar over a known total, the two figures under it, aria-busy on the region, and the list of what may and may not be done while it runs.
Created, updated, not posted and the total, the rejected-rows download, whether this can be undone, what a second run of the same file would do, and the route into the register.
Opaque, top-bordered, stuck to the bottom of the scrolling column: the contract line on the left, Back and the stage's primary on the right.

behaviour: Each stage validates before it advances and the primary names what it will do — Continue to mapping, Review the 37 problems, Post 1,203 rows — rather than saying Next four times.

A required field with nothing mapped to it blocks the mapping stage. The primary carries a real disabled attribute, because the reason is a fact rather than a policy, and it points at the sentence naming the field with aria-describedby; both come off together the moment the field is mapped, since a description that is display:none is read to nobody.
Two columns mapped to the same field is an error and is shown on both rows, not on whichever one was touched last.
The problem list filters by kind through a select rather than by row through a search box. Row numbers are how a failure is found in the spreadsheet, not how it is understood.

Fixing a value re-validates the whole staged file rather than the row it was typed into, and the new counts are announced from a role="status" that was already on the page. A fix that repairs 14 rows and reports only the one on screen is a fix nobody trusts.
The commit runs against a known total. The bar moves, the panel is aria-busy, milestones are announced every tenth, and nothing else on the stage is interactive except Cancel.

Cancel during a commit opens an alert dialog that states what is discarded in figures, because the answer differs by contract: under all-or-nothing the 742 rows already written go, under partial they stay.
The result stage is reached by a redirect, so refreshing it re-reads a finished run instead of importing the file a second time.
A second upload of a corrected file resumes at the review stage with the same mapping applied, so a user sent back to the spreadsheet does not pay for the mapping twice.
Nothing scrolls sideways at 390px. The mapping grid becomes one card per column, the preview and problem tables become stacked rows, and the footer buttons go full width in DOM order.
accessibility: One <main>, one <h1>, and it survives every stage. Panels below it are h2 and problem groups inside them h3, so the heading outline reads as the stages of one task rather than as five unrelated pages.

The stage nav is an <ol> inside a named <nav>, not a tablist. These are stages of one job rather than views of one record, so the current one carries aria-current="step"; a tablist would promise arrow-key movement between panels that do not exist.
Every stage change moves focus to the new stage's heading, which is tabindex="-1" for that reason. Focus left on the button that has just changed what it means tells a screen reader nothing happened.

The file input is a real input hidden with sr-only rather than display:none, and the focus outline is drawn on its label with peer-focus-visible. A display:none input cannot be focused and the keyboard never reaches the picker at all.

Every select in the mapping grid carries an aria-label naming its source column, because the same grid is rendered twice — a table above md and cards below it — and one for/id pair cannot serve two copies of a control. A <th scope="col"> establishes the column for anything reading the table as a table and contributes nothing to the accessible name of a control that has been tabbed to.

The count of what will and will not post is a role="status" that is in the document from first paint, so re-validating writes into a region that was already there. A live region that arrives with its message already inside it is announced to nobody.

The commit bar is role="progressbar" with aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax and a name pointed at the heading above it, plus aria-valuetext because the reading is rows rather than per cent. It takes no aria-live and no tabindex — it reports, and Cancel beside it acts.
aria-busy sits on the panel that is waiting and comes off the moment the run stops, whether it stopped by finishing or by failing.

The cancel dialog is role="alertdialog" with aria-modal, a focus trap, Escape closing it and focus returning to the trigger, and it states the figure it is about to discard in its body rather than in its title.
A problem group is a <section> with its heading as the accessible name and the rule in a paragraph the group's table is described by, so the rule is read once on entry instead of once per row.
The rejected-rows download is a link with a name saying how many rows and what format — "Download the 37 rejected rows as XLSX" — because Download three times on one screen names nothing.
Figures carry tabular-nums everywhere, so a count that falls from 37 to 21 after a fix does not reflow the line it sits in.

The file

Drag the spreadsheet here or XLSX or CSV · up to 20 MB · up to 5,000 rows
  • The first row is read as the header. One sheet per file — a workbook with three tabs imports the first and says nothing about the other two, so split it before uploading.
  • Format date columns as dates in the sheet. Excel stores 04 Sep 2026 as the number 45,904, and a column left as General arrives here as five digits.
  • Rate and quantity columns hold digits only. The currency and the unit are already known, so ₹118.40/kg is not a number this import can read.

What this import does

Download the template (XLSX)

  • Rows are matched on the item code. A code that already exists is updated; one that does not is created. Nothing is ever deleted by an import, and an item missing from the file is left alone.

  • Every row posts together. Nothing appears in the item master until all of them have. If you would rather post the good rows and deal with the rest afterwards, that is a choice you make at the review stage against a count.

  • The file is not kept. It is staged while you work through these stages and deleted after 7 days. The records it creates are what survives — to keep the vendor's own document, attach it to the rate contract instead.

While this runs

Stop the import?

The 742 rows already written stay in the item master — they were committed one at a time, and stopping does not take them back. The remaining 461 are not posted. The file stays staged, and running it again picks up from row 743.

Before you run anything else

  • Running this file again will not duplicate anything. The item code is the key, so the 1,118 it created would be updated rather than created twice. That is not the same as harmless: a second run overwrites the rate on all 1,203 items, including any that somebody has changed by hand since 11:52.

  • There is no single action that undoes this. Each of the 85 updates kept its previous rate in the item's price history, so the old figures are readable and a rate can be put back one item at a time. The 1,118 new items can be deactivated in bulk from the register.

  • The file is deleted on 28 Aug 2026. This screen keeps the counts and the rejected rows; it does not keep the spreadsheet. If the vendor's own document has to be kept, attach it to the rate contract.
